correctness.rationale: From \(\sigma(q)(p+1)=2pq\) with odd \(p,q\), the right side has 2-adic valuation one, so \(\sigma(q)\) is odd and therefore odd \(q\) is a square. Thus \(q\le10^{18}\) is exhaustively reduced to odd roots \(m\le10^9\). The packaged verifier factors every root by a segmented sieve, computes \(\sigma(m^2)\) exactly, and tests \(d=2m^2-\sigma(m^2)>0\) together with \(d\mid\sigma(m^2)\). Its complete output contains only the trivial pair and Descartes' pair. The computation was replayed from the actual package path.

originality.rationale: Tóth's peer-reviewed theorem stops at \(10^{12}\). The closest located public extension is a 2023 Mathematics Stack Exchange computation through \(10^{16}\), explicitly using the square reduction. The new exhaustive cutoff \(10^{18}\) is 100 times larger than that public computational frontier and one million times Tóth's published cutoff. The broader spoof-factorization literature does not state an ordinary-component bound of this size, and exact/semantic searches located no covering result.
residual_risks: A non-indexed private or public computation may already exceed the located \(10^{16}\) frontier.

value.rationale: The cutoff is the natural quantitative invariant singled out by Tóth's theorem, not an arbitrary slice. The result raises the peer-reviewed lower bound by six orders of magnitude and the closest located public computational bound by two orders of magnitude. The square reduction also changes the search dimension from all odd \(q\) to roots \(m\), making the extension reproducible in seconds while still exhaustively covering the full claimed interval. This is a meaningful finite boundary for the only known positive Descartes-number construction.
